nodes.name: On-site gas turbine manufacturers and service providers
nodes.mechanism: Data center operators buy gas turbines and long-term service contracts to generate power behind the meter, shifting revenue from utilities to turbine OEMs.
nodes.logic: Order intake rises as data center developers choose on-site generation to avoid interconnection delays and utility capacity charges. Service agreements tied to operating hours create recurring revenue that compounds with each additional unit installed.

nodes.name: Transmission and distribution equipment manufacturers
nodes.mechanism: Utility capital expenditure below replacement rates cuts orders for transformers, switchgear, cables, and other grid equipment.
nodes.logic: Utilities defer replacement and expansion projects, reducing volume for equipment makers whose sales track utility capital budgets. The decline is amplified because aging infrastructure would normally require accelerating replacement spend.

nodes.name: Regulated electric utilities with grid investment plans
nodes.mechanism: Slower rate base growth and flat load reduce allowed revenue and earnings growth under cost-of-service regulation.
nodes.logic: Regulated returns are applied to rate base, so below-replacement capex trims the asset base that earns an authorized return. Efficiency gains lower kilowatt-hour sales, further reducing volumetric revenue.

nodes.name: Behind-the-meter power and microgrid integrators
nodes.mechanism: Data center operators pay integrators to design and install on-site gas generation, controls, and islanding capability.
nodes.logic: Projects require engineering, procurement, construction, and commissioning beyond the turbine package itself. The complexity of paralleling with the grid creates demand for specialized integration.

nodes.name: Natural gas utilities and midstream providers serving data center gas turbines
nodes.mechanism: On-site gas-fired generation increases contracted gas delivery volumes and pipeline lateral demand.
nodes.logic: Data center gas turbines require firm transportation and local distribution connections, creating new throughput for utilities and midstream operators. This demand is independent of electric load growth.

nodes.name: Gas turbine component and aftermarket parts suppliers
nodes.mechanism: Higher turbine orders pull through demand for blades, combustion systems, coatings, and replacement parts.
nodes.logic: OEMs outsource complex components and use proprietary aftermarket networks, so volume increases at the component level. Running hours rise with installed capacity, accelerating maintenance part consumption.

nodes.name: Data center electrical distribution equipment suppliers
nodes.mechanism: Each on-site gas turbine campus requires medium voltage switchgear, busway, transformers, and UPS systems.
nodes.logic: Data center capex shifts from utility interconnection upgrades to behind-the-meter campus electrical infrastructure. Suppliers of power distribution equipment capture the same project budget that would otherwise go to utility-owned assets.

nodes.name: Utility transmission and distribution construction and field service contractors
nodes.mechanism: Lower grid equipment orders translate into fewer installation, upgrade, and maintenance contracts.
nodes.logic: Contractors depend on utility capital budgets and vendor delivery volumes for project starts. Reduced T&D equipment procurement signals fewer substation and line projects.

nodes.name: Power electronics and power conversion equipment suppliers
nodes.mechanism: Behind-the-meter gas and microgrid projects require inverters, converters, switchgear, and synchronization controls.
nodes.logic: Each installation includes electrical balance of plant that uses power electronics to manage power quality and islanding. The shift to on-site generation increases content per megawatt relative to grid-only supply.

nodes.name: Gas compression and pipeline equipment suppliers
nodes.mechanism: Higher gas deliveries to data center turbines require expansions in compression, metering, and pipeline lateral capacity.
nodes.logic: Midstream operators invest in incremental compression and measurement to serve firm transportation contracts. This equipment demand follows the gas supply buildout rather than electric load.

nodes.name: Smart meter and grid modernization equipment vendors
nodes.mechanism: Lower utility capex leads to deferred advanced metering and grid modernization programs.
nodes.logic: Utilities use discretionary capital for AMI and grid modernization, which is often delayed when budgets tighten. Vendor order pipelines thin as rate base growth slows.

nodes.name: Specialty alloy and casting suppliers for gas turbine hot sections
nodes.mechanism: Component makers buy nickel alloys, superalloys, and investment castings to produce turbine blades and combustion parts.
nodes.logic: Hot section components require alloys that withstand high temperatures, and capacity is limited. Rising component demand tightens supply and supports pricing.

nodes.name: Power semiconductor suppliers for power conversion and control
nodes.mechanism: Inverters and converters require IGBTs, MOSFETs, and diodes for high power switching.
nodes.logic: The shift to behind-the-meter generation increases the number of power conversion stages per installation. Power semiconductor content rises with the need for precise frequency and voltage control.

nodes.name: Utility construction equipment rental providers
nodes.mechanism: Fewer T&D construction and maintenance projects reduce demand for bucket trucks, cranes, and specialty tools.
nodes.logic: Rental fleets serve contractors and utilities directly, so utilization falls when project starts decline. Lower utilization pressures rental rates and fleet expansion plans.
